newsitem.title: USA: Clinton puts forward new pension protections.
newsitem.headline: Clinton puts forward new pension protections.

text.p: President Clinton Tuesday plans to announce ways to make it easier for workers to protect their retirement savings when they change jobs, the White House said in a statement.
The statement said the Treasury Department has taken steps to help workers with retirement savings roll them over into a new employer's pension plan. It does so in two ways:

First, it removes a barrier to such "rollovers" by stating in administrative guidance that a qualified pension plan that accepts a rollover that subsequently proves to be invalid will not be disqualified if the plan had reasonably concluded that the money involved was eligible.

The White House said many companies are now reluctant to accept such rollovers for fear their pension plans might be disqualified or penalised for inadvertently accepting funds that prove to be ineligible because a worker's existing pension plan was not tax-qualified or because the rollover was not completed within the 60-day period often required.

Second, the Treasury Department has transmitted a proposed regulation to make clear that accepting rollovers from new workers will generally not hurt a pension plan's ability to meet non-discrimination requirements. These requirements prohibit plans from providing benefits that discriminate in favour of highly paid employees.

The Treasury has also issued administrative guidance to ensure that employees who choose to leave their pension money with their former employer's retirement plan will not have their investment choices taken away from them.

The White House said the guidance makes clear pension plans that make a broad range of investment choices available to active employees may not limit former workers to investment in a money market fund.

Clinton was expected to discuss the moves, which build on pension reforms included in the minimum wage law signed last month, at the White House before setting off on a four-day campaign trip to the Midwest and the West Coast.
